3519. SHRI ANANTRAY DEVS HANKER DAVE: Will the Minister 
of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether cotton is growing in huge quantity in Gujarat; 
(b) whether the farmers do not get adequate price of cotton; 
(c) whether the Central Government purchased cotton of Rs. 11 crores 
from Gujarat but the payment has not been made to them; 
(d) whether Government propose to enhance the rate of cotton so that 
farmers may not be frustrated; and 
173 

 
       RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2000] 
 
(e) if not, in what way the Government propose to safeguard the 
interests of cotton growing farmers?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) to (e) Gujarat is one of the 
major cotton growing states in India. During last cotton season 1998 -99 
(October-September) 47 lakh bales (of 170 kg. each) of cotton was produced. 
As per estimates of the Cotton Advisory Board (in its meeting held on 
10.3.2000) the production during the current cotton year 1999- 2000 in 
Gujarat is likely to be 35 lakh bales. To safeguard the interests of the cotton 
growing farmers, the Government announces Minimum Support  Price (MSP) 
for Kapas (seed cotton) every year taking into account costs of all inputs and 
a reasonable margin of profit. In the event of the market price of Kapas falling 
below the MSP, the Cotton  Corporation of India Ltd. (CCI), a Public Sector 
Undertaking of the Government of India, purchases Kapas at MSP without 
any quantitative limit thus ensuring remunerative prices,to the cotton growing 
farmers. During the current cotton season 1999 -2000 market prices of Kapas 
in Gujarat have been ruling well above the MSP which implies that the 
farmers are receiving reasonable price for their produce. The Central 
Government does not purchase cotton, however, the CCI purchases cotton as 
a part of its commercial operation. During the current cotton season 1999-
2000, the CCI has so far (as on 11.4.2000) purchased 91,394 bales valued at 
Rs. 81.15 crore of cotton and there is no delay in payment to the farmers

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Difficulties faced by Institute of Gandhian Studies, Varanasi 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I wish to draw 
your attention and, through you, the attention of the Government to the sad 
state of affairs prevailing in the Institute of Gandhian Studies, Varanasi, an 
institute of national importance which was founded by the late Shri 
Jayaprakash Narayan. For the last nine months, the Indian Council of Social 
Science Research, at the behest of the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development, has stopped the release of normal grants that the ICSSR makes 
to this institution. Un der the present system, the ICSSR grants are linked to 
what the U.P Government gives. Because the ICSSR has stopped the grants, 
the U.P Government has not released funds and the work of the Institute has 
been paralysed. Sir, it has appeared in the newspapers that it is a part of an 
180 

[ 26 April, 2000 ] RAJYA SABHA 
attempt, ultimately, to get the Institute deregistered and to take over. This is 
also being done at the behest of some members of the faculty who face 
serious charges of misconduct and indiscipline. Sir. sometime ago, allegations 
were made that in this Institute, there was corruption and there was financial 
mismanagement. The Indian Council of Social Science Research appointed a 
committee to investigate these. Two representatives of the ICSSRwer e on that 
committee, and a representative of the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development was also there. That committee's report has exonerated the 
Institute of the charges of financial mismanagement. Yet, the Government is 
not releasing the grants, nor has  the Government thought it fit to make that 
report public. A representation has been made to the hon. President of India, 
and representations have also been made to the Prime Minister of India. I am 
told that at their intervention, a part of the grant is being released but in an 
inadequate manner. The grant is not being released and not being sent to the 
Institute, but it is being sent to the U.P Government to enable the payment of 
salary to the staff. I am told that no payment is being made to the Director. 
Sir, the way in which the HRD Ministry is interfering in the affairs of 
this Institute of national importance, the way it is preparing a ground for its 
deregistration and, ultimately, take- over of this Institute of national importance 
is a matter of seri ous concern. I would like the hon. Minister of Human 
Resource Development to enlighten the House as to what are his intentions in 
this matter. 
PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Mr-Chairman, 
Sir, with your permission, I would like to associate mys elf with the Special 
Mention made by Dr. Manmohan Singh. Sir, academicians in India are facing 
a severe problem. Even the assured financial assistance is not coming. Of 
course, we are wondering whether there is a design behind the whole scheme 
of not letti ng the academic institutions, well -known internationally recognised 
institutions to work properly. Even in West Bengal, the Institute of Historical 
Studies, a very old institute, is not getting the assured normal grant. We 
cannot but think that there is a definite motive behind this sort of red-tapism, 
prevention and deliberate obstacle in the way of research. The Institute of 
Gandhian Studies, which is a very, very reputed and respected organisation, 
has been mentioned by Dr. Manmohan Singh. 1 would reques t the Ministry of 
Human Resource Development, through you. Mr. Chairman, Sir, to release 
grants and give assistance to institutes like the Historical Studies, the History 
Congress and also give assistance to deserving 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [ 26 April, 2000 ] 
academicians so that they can concentrate on research and academic work 
without worrying about normal grants and without wondering about what the 
motive behind all this is. Thank you. 
SHRI ARJUN SINGH (Madhya Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, Sir, the 
Leader of the Opposition has put his finger on a very important and sensitive 
issue which I believe goes to the very root of what we are facing today. He has 
been generous to give all the good constructions to it while expressing his 
doubts. But I would like to say in a c lear language about this effort whether it is 
with the Institute of Gandhian Studies -or with any other academic institution 
which had a history - which was founded by no less a person than late 
Jayaprakashji. I think the significance of this name is not l ost on the hon. 
Members sitting opposite. This is the same Jayaprakashji whom you 
considered that he was leading the country into another era - which he did. But 
the fact is that in any area where the freedom of thought matters, where 
convictions matter, where the nation's polity has to be sensitised, each one of 
them is under attack, and an invidious attack sometimes on the pretext of 
inquiries, sometimes on the pretext of academic re-examination. And here is a 
case where the grants have been stopped altogether. I wish the hon. Minister 
of Human Resource Development stopped treating these institutions as happy 
hunting grounds. They are not. They are the institutions of the nation. We feel 
a sense of responsibility to them. If he feels they are not doing the ir work well, 
there are ways of going about it. But, if their effort is to decimate institutions 
one by one and in a manner which is totally alien to a democratic set -up, then, 
I think, a protest is needed, a loud protest is needed. Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
would like to request you that you must give some opportunity to this House to 
go into this matter in depth so that later there is no excuse given that when the 
voice had to be raised, it could not be raised and the people who want to 
trample every single institution, what I may call, the sinews from which a nation 
goes strong, should not be allowed to do that. This is my humble request. With 
these words, I associate myself with the issue raised by the Leader of the 
Opposition. 
SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI (Uttar Pra desh): Sir, the Leader of the 
Opposition has raised a very important issue. He raised it in a very sober and 
scholarly manner. In my personal capacity, I am also aware of the working of 
this institute. Much before this contioversy arose, I went there. That  is why I 
thought I would associate myself with what the hon. Leader of Opposition has 
said.  There are two sides of this issue, but I do not want to go into it. The 
182 

[ 26 April, 2000 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Director, Shri Nirmal Prasad, is a personal friend of mine. He explained his 
viewpoint. 1 do not know what the other viewpoint is, though I have seen both 
the viewpoints in various newspapers. In my own way, I was also making 
small efforts to see to it that these issues are resolved. At one time, I was of 
some help, so far as the U.P.Government was concerned. But 1 am really 
concerned. That is why I am with the hon. Leader of the Opposition that the 
matter, the question of dispute, the controversy about this, should be resolved 
soon, whether it is by the ICCR or whether it is by the ICSSR or whether it is 
by the Ministry of Education or whether it is by the U.P Government. Shri Arjun 
Singh himself was an Education Minister. One will have to harp back to many 
of the things that he did or he tried to do, which I do not propose to do. But 
what he has said "trampling the rights", etc. etc., I think give a different colour 
altogether. Then, naturally, one has to speak in that language. But 1 do not 
want this discussion to come down from the sublime to the ridiculous.  It is 
really amazing, but I am very happy to see that he has suddenly developed 
some respect, for late Jayaprakash Narayan. I think it is never too late to 
mend. Still I have a number of clippings from "Sunday ",of what he had said at 
different times, duri ng that particular period. That is why, I would like to say 
what Dr. Manmohan Singh has stated about the matter, which related to the 
academic standards of this country and the research institutions of this 
country, should not be diluted, should not be distorted. Considering the spirit in 
which he has said it, I fully associate myself with what Dr. Manmohan Singh 
has said that the research institutions must get assistance and there should 
not be any needless intervention by any outside agencies. But to say that this 
is an attempt at safronising and so on and so forth, will naturally create a 
controversy. That is why, Sir, except what has been added thereafter by 
another colleague of Dr. Manmohan Singh, I associate myself with what Dr. 
Manmohan Singh has said. There are two sides to this; I know something of 
both the sides, but I have to verify all the things. I have heard one side fully. I 
have got all the documents. Therefore, in this spirit, I associate myself with 
this, but not in the way in which an attem p has been made to give it an 
altogether different and controversial colour because of personal propositions. 
Thank you, Sir.

Agitation by Asstt. Professors working on Ad hoc basis in A.I.I.M.S. 
DR. Y. RADHAKRISHNA MURTY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, 
Sir, I thank you for giving me permission to make my Special Mention. My 
Special Mention pertains to one of the major premier medical institutions of our 
country. We had the bitter experience of strike by various categories of the 
staff of Delhi hospitals sometime back and the long suffering the patients had 
to undergo. The Ministry of Health had taken weeks and weeks to resolve 
those differences and the strike came to an end. Now, we have got the 
information that about 100 Asstt. Professors in the All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences, AIIMS as it is called, are in an agitational mood because all the 
hundred posts of Asstt. Professors are said to be on an ad hoc basis from 
September, 1993 onwards. No post has been filled up on a permanent basis. 
They have been filling up these posts bas ed on the bio-data of the candidate 
and at the discretion of the management. These doctors were appointed as 
Asstt. Professors temporarily for three months; and then they extend their 
tenure for another six months. From 1993 onwards, this has been going on. By 
this, the doctors are put to two disadvantages. One disadvantage is, whenever 
employment opportunities come from outside for them to enter, they are 
choosing the post of Asstt. Professor in AIIMS, even though it is temporary. 
They are doing it because this is a premier medical institution and a reputed 
hospital; and also with the fond hope that they would be absorbed in course of 
time. Therefore, they are reluctant to join other institutions. Finally, they are 
hanging in the mid air. Secondly, the facilities for research work in 
189 

RAJYA SABHA     [ 26 April, 2000 ] 
the hospital for which funds are available from the Department of 
Biotechnology, the Department of Science and Technology and also from the 
Indian Council of Medical Research and some other major medical institutions 
are being denied to the Asstt. Professors because most of them are working on 
an ad hoc basis; they are temporary. So, funds are being denied to these 
doctors. So much so, this major institution is starving for want of funds for 
research work. This is one major drawback which I wanted to bring to your kind 
notice. But the more important thing is regarding the patients who come and go 
without getting any medical care because these doctors are working on a 
temporary basis. Out of the 450 posts in this hospital, 100 posts are on an ad 
hoc basfs. Therefore, there is always a shortage of doctors. Thousands of 
patients are coming from far off places. They are standing in serpentine 
queues. They stand for hours and hours to get their chance. I have been told 
that already some of the important surgeries have been postponed due to lack 
of sufficient staff in the hospital. The plea of the management or the Ministry of 
Health is, "There is a court case pending." The House will be surprised to know 
that for the last seven years, the case is pending in the court. It is for the 
management of the institution or the Ministry of Health which is in charge of 
these institutions, to approach the Court to clear off the cases as early as 
possible. I think if they brought forth this particular point and the importance of 
the institution and the importance of medical aid to thousands and thousands 
of patients, the Court would have taken it very kindly and given its verdict very 
soon. I have got a feeling--I do not know the fact —that these two, the 
management and the Ministry, are not very keen on resolving this problem and 
therefore, the institution as well as hundreds of doctors are facing these 
problems. Hence, it is my earnest request to the Ministry of Health, particularly, 
to see that the cases are resolved and the difficulties of doctors as well as 
patients are avoided. Thank you.

wish to raise and bring to the notice  of the Government the fact that some 
more fishermen are there in Pakistani jails. We extend our gratitude to our hon. 
Prime Minister and the hon. Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu for taking efforts to

revealed to us. There are m ore people in Pakistani jails. It must be the 
concern of our Government now. After interviewing them, some information

SHRI N. THALAVAI SUNDARAM (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice -Chairman, 
Sir, thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak on the Motion of Thanks 
on the President's Address. I would like to bring to the notice of the House two 
statements. One statement is made by the President in his Address in the 
Central Hall of Parliament on the 50th Anniversary of the Constitution. It says, 
"Today when there is so much talk about revising the Constitution or even 
writing a new Constitution, we have to consider whether it is the Constitution 
that has failed us or whether it is we who have failed the Constitution. 
That was the speech made by the President in the Central Hall of 
Parliament. On the same day, the Prime Minister made a speech. He said, 
"There is one great test for Constitution. For any system of governance, it must 
deliver and it must be durable. Our Constitution has stood this test. One reason 
it has been able to do so is that it embodies a masterly balance between the 
rights of the individual and the requirements of collective life, between the 
States and the Union, and between providing a robust structure and flexibility. 
Our Constitution has served the needs of both India's diversities and her innate 
unity. It has strengthened India's democratic traditions." 
This was the speech of the Prime Minister of India marking the 50th 
Anniversary of the Constitution in the Central Hall of Parliament. Just a few 
weeks later, this Government drafts an Address for the President. The same 
Government and the Cabinet headed by the same Prime Minister, makes the 
President to come to the Central Hall with the Address and tell the nation that 
we feel that a review of the Constitution is necessary. 
I would like to quote a speech which was delivered by the hon. 
Member, Shri Nariman in the M.N. Roy Memorial Lecture-2000. It is a beautiful 
analysis of why the Constitution review is a dangerous thing. He said, "I would 
humbly say to our leaders in governance: Put aside your election manifesto . 
Cherish the Ideals of those who framed our Constitution. Do not, I beseech 
you, tamper with our Constitution by undertaking an overall review. Such a 
venture can only lead to rising expectations, then dissatisfaction and 
disillusionment, followed by frus tration and perhaps even ultimate 
disintegration."

please look at this issue once again and do not take a wrong step. Sir, the

In what way will it be helpful to our country? The representatives of the people 
are running the Government. What is the necessity for the review of the 
Constitution? This is my fir st point. The statement made by the President is

DR. A. R. KIDWAI (Delhi): Sir, we are grateful to the President for his 
Address to the Joint Session. But I find that there is an important omission 
regarding the Services. For any Government, the Services represent a very 
important section; in fact, the administration, the working of the Government, 
entirely depends on the services. That is why  Part XIV of the Constitution 
entirely is devoted to the services and their management, their career, their 
security of service so that they can serve the country objectively, impartially, 
with integrity. That is, why it was necessary that seme considerati on should 
have been given and mention should have been made about the Services. 
When India became free, we adopted the British model of civil services. The 
hallmark of the British civil service is the neutrality of the services, which is 
impartial, objective and characterised by its integrity: It is not aligned with any 
political party or any group or any shade of opinion. The members of the 
services are trained professionally, they are professionals specialising in 
general administration, police, law and order, revenue; in all aspects of 
services. Therefore, as professionals, they should serve the Government with 
competence, without any tinge of alignment with political parties, associations, 
groups or any individuals. This was the model adopted by our leaders when 
India became free. These services acquitted themselves, did well in the 
consolidation of our princely States, in establishing, a stable administration in 
the country and running the affairs well. They are committed to the 
Constitution, they are committed to the administrative discipline and 
philosophy. However, we find that during the last fifty years, there has been an 
erosion in the training programmes, in their career Civil Servants development, 
in their attitude of neutrality objectivity and im partiality. Specially, in    the     
States     where     the   civil   servant* are   transferred   on   the 
200 

[26 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
basis of likes or dislikes, the postings sometimes depend on the basis of caste 
and creed considerations. Now,  there is even more politicisation of the 
services. Members of the Civil Services are now stamped or treated as closely 
associated to particular views and shades of opinion, political parties and, 
more so, even with individuals. Now, this hampers their functioning as Civil 
Servants. The functions of Civil Servants are quasi judicial and if they are 
impartial in their objective they enjoy greater respect and confidence of the 
people. The success of a Government depends on the objectivity and this 
impartiality of the Services so that they can inspire the people. The more these 
services enjoy the confidence of the people, the greater is the success of the 
Government. These are very important aspects which should be respected. 
Gradually these are being eroded. T he postings have assumed the form of 
musical chairs. The way even the most competent officers are shunted or 
sidelined or neglected because they belong to a different caste or creed and so 
on, has created great discontent in the services. And they do not get justice in 
their own Ministries and Departments. Why are there so many cases going to 
courts? Why is there the necessity to set up the Central and State 
Administrative Tribunals? This is a sign of dissatisfaction among the services. 
This is a sign of la ck of discipline in the services. If the Ministries and the 
Departments are not able to do justice to their employees and they have to go 
to courts or tribunals, that shows the Departments are not working properly and 
this is not a healthy sign. The public  expects to get justice from these 
Departments which cannot do justice to their own employees. These are some 
of the important considerations. Then, there is a greater confusion with the 
proliferation of services. When India became free, there were only 11 2 
Secretaries to the Government. Today, there are nearly 4000 Secretaries to 
the Government. There was no cadre of Joint Secretaries then. I am sorry. The 
Secretaries are about 400 instead of 112. There was no cadre of Joint 
Secretaries. Today there are about 4,000 Joint Secretaries to the Government. 
The number of Civil Servants is more than the posts that are available. 
Sometimes they get corridor postings; they run up and down the corridor to get 
a proper post. Therefore, I feel after 50 years of our car eer management, we 
have not been successful. The way we manage the careers of such a large 
number of administrative services in the Department of Personnel it is not 
professional; it is not adding any professional content to the management of 
the services.  That is why it is necessary that measures must be taken to 
maintain the quality, neutrality and impartiality of the 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [ 26 April, 2000 ] 
services and the professional competence, through rigorous training and 
follow-up of career so that they can advance in their career, with the increasing 
changes and development in the society, maintaining the same objectives. 
These are some of the important considerations. At this stage of development, 
we should give a high consideration to this because no  Government can 
successfully perform without a good administrative service, which inspires 
public confidence and which enjoys the respect of the public. 
Thank you.

SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA (Orissa): Sir,.I rise to support the 
Motion of Thanks on the President's Address moved by Shri M. Venkaiah 
Naidu, but I do not agree at all with the points made by him while moving the 
motion. 
Many hon. Members have put  forward their views on the question of 
reviewing the Constitution and setting up of the Constitution Review 
Committee. In this connection I would like to say that the Indian Constitution is 
a good Constitution. As a trade union leader, I would like to say  that we have 
got as many as 147 Acts and Rules. Even many of the developed countries do 
not have such a large number of Acts and Rules. But, the problem is that we 
do not have the will to implement those Acts and Rules in right earnest. 
Therefore, I would say that instead of reviewing the Constitution, let us review 
the decisions and administration of policies of the Government. We should see 
whether we have been giving to the people the rights and benefits that the 
Constitution has envisaged. If you are not able to give that privilege to the 
people of India, I do not think we have the right to review anything that is 
contained in the Constitution. 
I come to my second point. Hon. Minister, Shri George Fernandes is 
here. He was the Chairman of the Apex Commi ttee set up to deal with the 
problems created by the Orissa Cyclone. There was a demand made by all the 
political parties of the country to Shri George Fernandes and to the Prime 
Minister that the Orissa cyclone should be declared as a national calamity of  
rare severity. The Prime Minister and the Defence Minister, Mr. George 
Fernandes, said, "No, we cannot declare it because there is no provision in the 
Famine Code, there is no provision in the Relief Code." Mr. Vice-Chairman, 
Sir, I want to put a question to the Government. About 25 lakh houses have 
been damaged, 10,000 people were killed, 1.5 million people were affected by 
the cyclone in 120 blocks, 12 districts. The whole country, the whole State, all 
political parties demanded that this cyclone should be declared as a national 
calamity of rare severity. They did not declare it. They did not amend the 
Famine Code. They did not amend the Relief Code. In spite of the distress 
situation, they could not amend the famine code, they could not amend the 
relief code. It was not a statute. It doesn't require a two-thirds majority in both 
Houses to amend it. We could have done it. Just

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
*461. [The questioner (Shri Bratin Sen Gupta) was absent. For answer, 
vide page 22 infra.] 
Visit by Australian Foreign Minister to India 
*462. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the 
Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that the Australian Foreign Minister visited India 
recently; 
(b) if so, what is the outcome of his visit; and 
(c) whether he indicated restoration of normalcy after the Pokhran Test 
in 1998? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. The Australian Foreign Minister Mr. Alexander Downer 
visited India from 21—24 March, 2000.  
(b) Mr. Downer called on the President and PM and separately met me  
and the Minister of Commerce and Industry. A range of bilateral and 
multilateral issues were discussed. Both countries agreed, in principle, to 
resume defence  relations. Mr. Downer exte nded me an invitation to visit 
Australia, which I have  accepted: With Shri Murasoli Maran Mr. Downer 
discussed issues relevant to Commerce and Industry. 
(c) Yes, Sir. Both sides agreed, in principle, to resume the defence 
relations which were broken off after the Pokhran tests in 1998. Modalities for 
this will be worked out.

[27 April, 2000]           RAJYA SABHA 
Research on preservation of foodgrains and vegetables 
*464. SHRI K.M KHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) 
has carried out some research for preservation for foodgrains and vegetables; 
(b) if so, what extent this technology is being used in the country; 
(c) whether use of such technology for preservation of foodgrains and 
vegetables is safe and good for human life; and 
(d) if so, what specific proof Government have and what are the details 
thereof? 
THE MINISTER Of STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC 
ENERGY (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid 
on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) has carried 
out extensive research for preser vation of meat & meat products, spices, 
foodgrains, viz, rice, wheat & wheat products, semolina (sooji, rawa) and 
vegetables viz. potatoes, onions, garlic, ginger, mushrooms etc. 
(b) After considerable R&D in this field, a small Pilot Scale Package 
Irradiator which can treat up to 500 kg of onion and potato per hour is being 
operated at Food Technology Division, Bhaba Atomic Research Centre, 
Mumbai. A facility for technology demonstration purpose has been 
commissioned by the Department of Atomic Energy for irradition of spices at 
Vashi, Navi Mumbai. Another demonstration facility for irradiation of 
potatoes, onions and other food products with need low dose irradiation is 
being set up at Lasalgaon in Nasik District of Maharashtra. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) The Ministry of Healt h and Family Welfare, Govt. of India, New 
Delhi has amended suitably the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules (1955) 
in 1994 and given clearance for radiation processing of food has also been 
accepted by the World Health Organisation, Food & Agriculture O rganisation, 
International Atomic Energy Agency and Codex Alimentarious Commission 
which is responsible for setting up global food standards. A number of 
countreis are already using the radiation process for a variety of foods. 
SHRI K.M. KHAN: Sir, this technology is a very important and useful 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [27 April, 2000] 
development in the preservation of food. I would like to ask the hon. Minister 
whether this technology can be made available throughout the country or it 
would be usedhonly in areas co nfined to atomic research centres. What are the 
difficulties faced by the Government in providing such vital facilities all over 
the country? 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, food security, as the hon. 
Member said, is a primaru importance for the self -reliance of any country. I do 
agree with it. This is one of the latest methods which has been developed for 
preserving food, with the least change in sensory quality. It involves exposure 
of food to short -wave energy, which allows you to extend its itshelf life,  
anything to do with insect disinfestation, anything which is carried like food 
borne pathogens and parasaites, as also anything like microbial decontamination 
of spices. It is eco -friendly. It consumes less energy. It has an operational 
simplicity, and it is the latest technology. 
Now, there are certain safety features that are to be followed, under this, 
the irradiation plants requires to be authorised by the Atomic Energy 
Regulatory Board. After this, the licence has to be obtained from the authority 
concerned — in this case, it is the Atomic energy Department — and it is to be 
issued only after ascertaining all the safety aspects of the installation and its 
suitability to ensure proper process controls, availability of licensed operations 
and qualified s taff. In some progressive States, the Food and Drug 
Administration also does this job. This is available, at the moment, in three 
Statas —  Goa, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh. We have a small pilot project, 
which is food package irradiator, at the Food Tec hnology Division of BARC, 
in Mumbai, which can treat about five hundred kg. of onion and potato. 
There is one more which is under construction at Laselgaon as Nasik in 
Maharashtra. As far at this is cboncerned, we would be happy that these come 
up in other parts of the country provided the safety standards are taken care of, 
met and stringent quality is maintained. 
SHRI K.M. KHAN: Sir, my second supplementary is that this issue 
relates to the safety aspects. I would like to know whether the foodgrains and 
vegetables undergone through the atomic rays are indeed safe for human 
consumption and no side effects are there by using such preserved foodstuffs. 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, the process itself involves 
passing the food through a radiation field which allows food sto absorb the 
desired radiatron energy and the studies that have been done show that this has 
very little effect on the nutrients itself. Sir, extensive studies on food irradiation  
8 

[27 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
have been conducted worldwide and experts of the WHO, FAO, international 
atomic energy agencies and we have jointly reviewed all the data that has been 
obtained worldwide, including from India, in the last four decades. They have 
declared that irradiated food is safe for human consumpt ion. The American 
Council for Science and Health, the American Medical Association, the 
National Institution of State Department of Agriculture, the Council of 
Agricultural Science and Technology and the American Dietetic Association 
have all endorsed the safety of the irradiated food. Today 38 other countries, 
apart from us, have approved the use of radiation in certain food items. 
DR. BIPLAB DASGUPTA: Sir, I fell that on this issue, I would say that 
we will be entering an unknown territory. We have been g iven a complete and 
impressive list of organisations and insitutions which have certified that this 
food is safe. But the point is that this is only one side of the picture. It is quite 
possible that the scientists from Britain may take a different positio n. I will 
give you a concrete example of genetically modify food. Now, America is 
trying to push genetically modified food all over the world. In Britain there is a 
lot of resistance to it. In fact, they are saying it is a right of the consumer to 
know whe ther it is genetically modified food or not and every shop has to 
advertise in this regard. Similarly, about the food which is subjected to 
radiation, we are yet to know its impacts. As you know, about nuclear energy it 
was said at one stage that it did no t affect environmentally, and all that. But 
later it was found that it pollutes the atmosphere in different ways. What I am 
asking is this. Is the hon. Minister satisifed with whatever has been told to her 
by the American establishment or has she been able to consult much more 
wider groups of scientists and technicians to know that this type of food is not 
contaminted by this process? 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, I am sure that the hon. 
Member's apprehension is something that probably is shared by a lot of people 
because this is a very new technology. As this is a new technology, at the 
moment, we are in the process of sensitising a lot of people about it. But, I can 
say that we will do our best and we will have a certain amount of interaction 
with all con cerned. What I have just now told you on the floor of the House 
means that there is a lot of interaction going on. As far as the Atomic 
Regulatory Board is concerned, it takes extreme and stringent steps to see that 
we keep it within the safety standards. We will do our best remain within those 
safety standards. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, in our country we have 
an Atomic Regulatory Authority. I would like to know from the hon. Minister  
9 

RAJYA SABHA [27 April, 2000] 
whether this matter of low irradiation has ever been referred to mis Atomic 
Regulatory Authority and whether they have certified with regard to its safety. 
The second question is that if the Minister is so sure that this is perfectly a safe 
technology, then why are we limitinjg its use only to a small pilot scale project? 
SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE: Sir, first, I will reply to the second 
part of the question. We have, very recently, after the testing which was 
conducted at the BARC, started two centres —one at Nasik and the other one at 
Navi Mumbai. These facilities are still coming up. They are expensive facilities. 
They have to go through some very stringent testing and that has taken a certain 
amount of time. Also, the food and drug authority itself, in the States, is at 
various stages  of progress. The three States that are very progressive are: 
Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Goa. The other States, as far as mis issue is 
concerned, are still formulating the laws and rules. A certain amount of time has 
taken place. As I said, this would be dealt with. 
With regard to the second part of the supplementary. I would submit that 
it has been referred to the AERB. The AERB has laid down a very stringent set 
of guidelines, and those guideliens are to be followed before the licence is 
issued by the Department of Atomic Energy.

Implementation of report of Bachhawat and Manisana Wage Board 
*467. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of LABOUR 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether recommendations of the Bachhawat Wage Board and 
Manisana Wage Board Reports were accepted by Government for 
implementation; 
(b) if so, date of submission of such report, recommendations accepted, 
date of issue of notification and implementation status of each 
recommendation in various States and Union Territories; and 
(c) the reasons for non -implementation of  such report in Assam and 
targeted action contemplated to ensure its early compliance? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (DR. SATYA NARAYAN JATTYA): 
(a) and (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the house.

Statement 
The report of th e Bachawat Wage Board was submitted to the 
Government on 30.5.1989. The recommendations regarding pay scales, 
dearness allowance, house rent allowance, city compensatory allowance etc. 
were accepted by Government vide notifications dated 31.8.89 and the ra tes 
of house rent allowance and city compensatory allowance were modified by 
notification dated 21.0990. The responsibility for implementation of 
recommendations lies with state Governments. As per information received 
from State Governments, out of 1715 n ewspaper establishments, 643 have 
fully implemented and 26 have partially implemented the recommendations. 
A statement showing position of implementation in various States/Union 
Territories is enclosed at Statement-I. (See below) 
As regards recommendations  of Manisana Wage Board, the final 
recommendations have not been submitted to the Government. In October, 
1995, the Manisana Wage Board submitted Interim Report recommending 15 
% of the basic wage as interim relief to all newspapers employees. The 
Government notified the interim relief vide Notifications dated 24.9.96 
giving interim relief at the rate of 20% of the basic wage and an additional 
amount of Rs. 100/- p.m. w.e.f 204.1995. 
The Manisana Wage Board submitted tentative proposals to the 
Government on 21.12.1999 which were published in the Gazette on 
30.12.1999. The employers' and employees' organisations and other persons 
interested in the revision of rates of wages were required to submit their 
comments with respect to tentative proposals., In respon se to the above 
notice, 72 parties submitted their comments and 42 requested for oral 
hearings. The oral hearings on comments/objections were completed in three 
rounds during February 22-25, March 14-17 and March 27-31,2000. 
The meetings of the Manisana Wage Board to finalise the report were 
held during 17th to 20b April, 2000. The Board is yet to submit final report. 
As per information received from the Government of Assam, the 
Bachawat Wage Board Award has been implemented by four newspaper 
estalishments namely, Assam Tribune, Dainik Asom, Janambhumi and the 
Sentinel Group of Papers, out of a total of 74 newspaper establishments. 
It has further been reported that in a tripartite meeting held on 
30.10.1999 between representatives of newspaper employees, employers and 
government officials, a decision was taken to ask newspaper establishments 
to determine

Remumeration of Contract Employees in PSUs 
*463. SHRI DIPLIP SINGH JUDEV: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that some public sector 
undertakings are appointing techni cal and non- technical persons as coatract 
employees on meagre remuneration; 
(b) if so, under what rules these employees are being engaged; 
(c) whether the service conditions of these employees are pitiable as  
compared to regular employees; and 
(d) if so, what step s Government propose to take to direct the various  
public sector undertakings for regularisation of the services of these contract 
employees with proper salaries, allowances and other facilities? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (DR SATYA NARAYAN JATIYA): 
(a) to (d) the Central Government have enacted the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 to protect the interests of contract 
labour engaged through contractors. It regulates the employment of contract 
labour in certain establishments and provides for  its abolition in certain 
circumstances. The Act and the rules made thereunder also provides for the 
regulation of conditions of work, payment of wages and other amenities 
relating to welfare and health of contract labour. 
The Contract Labour (Regulation and abolition) Central Rules, 1971 
provides that the rates of wages payable to the workmen of the contractor 
shall not be less than the rates prescribed under the Minimum Wages Act, 
1948 for such employment where applicable and where the rates have been 
fixed by agreement, settlement or award, not less titan the rates so fixed. In 
case, where the workman employed by the contractor performs the same or 
similar kind of work as the workmen directly employed by the p rincipal 
employer of the establishment, the wa ge rates, holidays, hours of work and 
other conditions of service of the workmen of the contractor shall be the same 
as applicable to the workmen directly employed by the principal employer of 
the establishment on the same or similar kind of work. In other  cases, the 
wage rates, holidays, hours of work and conditions of services of the 
workmen of the contractor shall be such as may be specified in this behalf by 
the Chief Labour Commissioner (Central). The data relating to payment of 
remuneration to contrac t workers by Central Public Sector Undertakings is 
not maintained centrally. However, complaints brought to the notice of the 
government regarding payment of less 
24 

[27 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
remuneration and pitiable conditions of contract labour are dealt with and 
appropriate action taken under the provisions of the Act and the rules. 
The Act does not provide for absorption of such labour on regular basis. 
In the aftermath of the judgement of the Supreme Court in Air India Statutory 
Corporations and O thers Vs. United Labour Union and Others, however, the 
establishments engaging contract labour are under statutory obligation to 
absorb contract labourers on regular basis wherever the "appropriate 
Government' by way of notification under section 10 of the  Contract Labour 
(Regulation and abolition) Act, 1970 have prohibited employment of contract 
labour in any job/work/ process in the establishment. The criteria to be 
adopted for absorption of such contract labour on regular basis as per the 
judgement will be the duration of work, number of employees working on the 
job etc. In case of retrenchment due to excess staff, the principle of "last 
come, first go' will be applied subject to reappointment as and when vacancy 
arises. 
The judgement of Hon' ble Supreme Court dated 6.12.96 in the case of 
Air India Statutory Corporations and Others Vs. United Labour Union and 
Others is the established law under Article 141 of the Constitution. It was 
published in 1997 LLR 288 and AIR 1997 SC 645. The implications of the 
judgement were examined in consultation with the Ministry of Law, Justice 
and Company Affairs and directions were issued to the emforcement agency 
of the Ministry of Labour to strictly implement the judgement in its letter and 
spirit.

Deficiency of Nutritious Substances in Soil 
*473. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: Will the Minister of AGRI CULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether due to intensive farming iron, zinc, sulphur and other such 
subtle nutritious substances are decreasing in soils of various regions; 
30 

[27 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details of the research done and the i nformation available 
in this regard; and 
(c) the effects apprehended on the health and production of various 
crops and plants due to the deficiency of these subtle nutritious substances? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SUNDER LAL 
PATWA): (a) Yes, Sir. The in tensive farming with high inputs and high 
yielding varieties have resulted into dificiencies of micro and secondary 
nutrients particularly zinc, sulphur and iron in different regions of the 
country. 
(b) The Institutes of ICAR and State Agricultural Univers ities have 
been undertaking basic strategic and applied research programmes to 
delineate micronutrient deficient areas, develop suitable diagnostic 
techniques, study responses of crops and to ameliorate micronutrient 
disorders in soils and plants.  These studies are coordinated through All India 
Coordinated Research Project  (AICRP) on Micronutrients in Soils and Plants 
of ICAR started in the year 1967. 
Analysis of about 2,00,000 samples from 15 States and two Union 
Territories showed that zinc (Zn) deficienc y is very widespread followed by 
sulphur (S) boron (B), iron (Fe), manganese (Mg), copper (Cu) and 
molybdenum (Mo) deficiences. 
(c) Since the secondary and micronutrients play very important role in  
the growth and development of plants, thier deficiencies result into the loss of  
productivity, stability and sustainability of crop yields.

Water wheel Turbine 
*477.  SHRI J.CHITHARANJAN: 
SHRI GAYA SINGH: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to a news -item 
appearing in the Economic Times, Delhi Edition, dated 12th March, 2000, 
under the caption "pump up the Volume" legarding the invention of a water 
wheel turbine that runs without fuel or electricity, by a UP farmer; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have any plan to help this inventor to start 
commercial production of this water wheel turbine; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SUNDAR LAL 
PATWA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A water wheel turbine has been developed by 
Shri Mangal Singh a farmer of village Bhailonilodh from district Lalitpur 
(UP). He also sought financial assistance from the Council for Ad vancement 
of Peoples' Action and Rural Technology (CAPART) under the Ministry of 
Rural Area & Employment, Govt. of India. The Water Wheel Turbine 
operates centrifugal pump(s), which can lift upto about 36 litres of water per 
second at 6.5 cm delivery head utilizing the hydrostatic energy of water by 
creating 1.8 meter water head using simple check dam in a flowing river or 
nala. The water current created pushes the paddles of the water wheel and 
rotates the wheel around its shaft, thus generating mechanical  power which is 
utilised to operate centrifugal pump(s). 
On the request of CAPART this water wheel turbine pump was 
inspected and assessed by the Scientists of Central Institute of Agricultural 
Engineering (CIAE), Bhopal during 1987 and in 1989. The perfor mance of 
the pump was found to be satisfactory although further refinements in the 
pump were recommended. It is learnt that Shri Mangal Singh has since 
obtained a patent of his water wheel turbine pump. It has been presented to 
International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) of Untied Nations in 
Rome who estimated system cost about Rs. 5.0 lakhs (at the price level of 
1998). Shri Mangal Singh wants that these be manufactured and installed for 
the benefit of the farmers.

imbalances in the level of production and productivity of various crops. The 
salient features of strategies are as follows: 
(a) Promoting cropping system approach of increasing the production 
and productivity of cereals crops as a whole against the individual 
crop approach. Encouragement will be given to follow green 
manuring and use of compost and other organic sources; 
(b) Encouraging varietal replacement and propagation of newer location 
specific High Yielding Varieties with biotic and abiotic resistance; 
(c) Improving the resource base of the farmers and encouraging devices 
for efficient water management for timely and effective field 
operations; 
(d) Popularisation of improved crop production technologie s through 
organisation of field demonstration as farmer's holdings and training 
of farmers and farm labourers including women; 
(e) Encouraging the integrated nutrient management for sustainable 
agricultural production; 
 
(f) Greater emphasis on the adoption of Inte grated Pest Management 
Approach to control the pests and diseases and also use of 
weedicides to control the weed menace to crops; 
(g) More emphasis on the proper adoption of non -monetary inputs like 
timely sowing, maintaining optimum plant population, efficien t use 
of fertiliser and need based plant protection measures; and

Dangerous Effects of Low level Nuclear Radiation 
3569. SHRI EDU ARDO FALEIRO: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that several countries are phasing out nuclear 
power stations after the Chernobyl and Three Mile incidents apart from 
scores of other lesser known incidents and health hazards caused to workers 
and nearby populations; 
(b) whether Government are aware that several recent studies have 
established the highly dangerous effects of low level nuclear radiation; and  
(c) if so, reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTM ENT OF ATOMIC 
ENERGY (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) Electricity generation 
by Nuclear Energy in the world increased by about 26% during the period 
1990— 99 as per information available. Although there has been slowing 
down in nuclear power capacity additi on in U.S.A., Canada and Western 
Europe, this is to be looked at in the context of their self -sufficiency in 
meeting the electricity demand with a high level of per capita electricity 
consumption, stagnant population growth as well as easy access to other 
energy sources. It cannot be attributed to safety reasons. Safety in Nuclear 
Power Plants are getting continously upgraded world over to meet emerging 
concerns from time to time including lessons learnt from Chernobyl and 
Three Mile Island Accident. The nu clear capacity addition is now centered in 
Asia. 
A study, based on International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) 
documents indicates that between the period 1990 to 1997 48 Nuclear Power 
Reactors were connected to the grid and as of the end of 1998,36 Nuclear 
Power Reactors with a net capacity of 27536 MWe are reported to be under 
construction. About 16% of the world electricity needs are being met through 
nuclear power reactors. 
(b) and (c) Studies on the biological effects of Nuclear Radiation have 
been in pr ogress in several research institutions for many decades. These 
studies have been analysed and summarised by the United Nations Scientific 
Committee on the effects of Atomic Radiation. Based on these studies, the 
International Commission on Radiological Pr otection — a specialist 
organisation — makes periodic recommendations on the safe use of radiation. 
In line with these recommndations, the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board 
issues appropriate safely directives to regurlate radiation exposure to radiation 
workers and members of the public in India.

3608. MISS. MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of LABOUR be  
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government will make a National Policy for Bidi 
Labourers so that they may get equal wages all over the country; 
(b) whether Government will take necessary steps to ensure that the

lower wages for Bidi making thereby rendering lakhs of bidi labourers

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) and (b) The Government has 
examined the issue of a National Wage Policy which has been discussed on 
many occasions in different fora. Since fixation of wages depends on a 
number of factors like local conditions, cost of living and paying capacity, 
which varies from State to State and from Industry to Industry, it has not been 
found feasible to maintain uniformity in wages all over the country. The 
Indian Labour Conference, held in November 1985 express ed that 'Till such 
time a national wage is feasible, it would be desirable to have regional 
minimum wages in regard to which the Central Government may lay down 
the guidelines. The minimum wages should be revised at regular periodicity 
and should be linked with rise in the cost of living." Accordingly, the 
Government issued guidelines in July, 87 for setting up of Regional Minimum 
Wages Advisory Committees. These Committees renamed subsequently as 
Regional Labour Ministers' Conferences, made a number of recommendations 
which include reduction in disparities in minimum wages in different states of 
a region, setting up of Inter -State Coordination Council and consultation with 
neighbourig States while fixing/ revising minimum wages. 
In the absence of a National  Wage Policy, the Central Government 
introduced National Floor Level Minimum Wage of Rs. 35/ - per day in 1996 
based on the recommendations of the National Commission on Rural Labour 
in 1991 and subsequent increase in price level. The Floor Level Minimum 
Wage was further enhanced to Rs. 40/- per day in August, 1998 when Hon'ble 
Prime Minister wrote to all the State Governments/Union Territories 
requesting them to ensure that minimum wages are not paid below Rs. 40/ - 
per day for any scheduled employment. It h as been further increased to Rs. 
45/- per day due to increase in the Consumer Price Index Number.

SPECIAL MENITONS 
         Non-Release of funds to Gram Panchayats for the years 1998-99 
and 1999-2000 as recommended by the Tenth Finance Commission 
SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh) 
Sir, I thank you for giving me t his opportunity to bring to the notice of this 
august House a very serious and urgent problem being faced by the Gram 
Panchayats. Sir, Panchayats are there since the 1960's, in almost all the States. 
But they are there only for name sake. No funds are give n to the Panchayats 
and no powers are given to them. The elections have not taken place in so 
many Panchayats for so many years. We are proud of the Seventy -third 
Constitutional Amendment which tries to regulate the functioning of the 
Panchayats and streng then them. The Seventy- third Constitutional 
Amendment of 1992 directs the State Government through article 243 (i) to 
constitute a Finance Commission to review the financial positions of the 
Panchayats and make recommendations to the Governor, as also thro ugh 
article 243 (g) to endow the Panchayats with such powers and authorities, as 
may be necessary, to enable them to function as institutions of self -
government. Even today most of the States are not giving the necessary 
powers to the Panchayats. Though they are not given the powers, they are the 
only approachable institutions by the poorest of the poor and those who are 
living in rural areas. The States are not giving the powers to the Panchayats 
and they are helpless. They can exercise powers only when th ey are given .to 
them. Now, they are compelled to beg those who are having powers. If the 
functioning of the Gram Panchayats are undermined, the roots of our 
democracy will be shaken. This is my submission to the House. 
Sir, the Tenth Finance Commission ha d taken into consideration the 
pathetic financial conditions of Gram Panchayats and was kind enough to 
make some recommendations. I quote from the recommendations: 
"We are making an ad hoc provision of Rs. 100 per capita 
of rural population. For all States  the figures are indicated 
at Annexure XI. This amount should be distributed amongst 
the panchayati raj institutions, over and above their due, by 
way of their share of the assigned taxes, duties, tolls, fees, 
transferred activity-related budgets and 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
grants. Even in those States which are not required to have 
panchayats, as envisaged in the 73rd amendment of the 
Constitution, the additional amounts would be required to 
be given to supplement the resources of similar local level 
representative bodies." 
According to this recommendation, all the States together should get 
from the Central Government an amount of Rs. 4,380.93 crores at the rate of 
Rs. 1,095 crores per year from 1996- 97 onwards, that is, for four years. The 
share of Andhra Pradesh for these four years is Rs. 351 crores at the rate of 
87.75 crores per year. The Central Government was kind enough to release 
the share of Andhra Pradesh for 1996 -97 and 1997- 98, but the share of Rs. 
175.5 crores for 1998- 99 and 1999- 2000 has not been released till date. 
Recently, a delegation from Andhra Pradesh came to Delhi and met our 
Minister of Rural Development, Mr. Sunderlal Patwa, and the Minister 
promised them to release the share of Andhra Pradesh for these two years by 
31st March, 2000. But, I am sorry to say that that amount has not been 
released till today. There are 21,934 Sarpanches in Andhra Pradesh. They are 
agitating. A week ago a delegation came here to request the Central 
Government to release the funds. Sir, I appeal, through you, to the hon. 
Finance Minister and the hon. Minister of Rural Development to release 
immediately the share of Andhra Pradesh for the years 1998 -99 and 1999-
2000, that is, an amount of Rs. 175.5 crores. I believe the same thing is 
happening in the case of other States also. The entire amount recommended 
by the Tenth Finance Commission should be released keeping in view the 
necessity of strengthening the functioning of the Gram Panchayats. 
Problems being faced by Telephone users' allottees and non attending of 
complaints by Telecom authorities in Time 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh) : Thank you, 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, for giving me this opportunity. The telephone connections 
have increased manifold in the country, particularly in Hyderabad. As a 
measure to face, the stiff competition from the private sector, the Telecom 
Department has been making efforts to increase connections in Hyderabad. 
With this, however, the problems of the consumers have also increased. 
Though new schemes were announc ed and the capacity of the exchanges has 
been increased, the consumers are 
152 

[ 27 APRIL, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
not getting the connections in time. The consumers are waiting for 
connections for months together. For example, the setting up of a new 
exchange in Uppahiru of Krishna district was announced and a building was 
constructed many' months ago. Still, it has not been opened and the people 
are awaiting connections. In Hyderabad, many people got the wiring done 
and also got the instruments, but connection was not given for months 
together. This is a peculiar situation with the Telecom Department. If we ask 
from a private company like Tata, in Hyderabad, they will give the 
connection the very next day. When will the Telecom Department become so 
prompt? Alth ough the Telecom Department had brought out the 
advertisement that within 24 hours, the complaints will be attended to; and 
within 25 days of the request shifting of phone will be done, yet these are 
delayed for days and months. I want the Government to ta ke necessary action 
and ensure better and prompt facilities to the consumers; otherwise the day is 
not far off when the private sector will overtake the Telecom Department.  
Thank you, Sir. 
MR. CHAIRMAN : Now, Shri Ravi Shankar Prasad. 
Non-Holding of Panchayat elections by State Governments every 
five years 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD (Bihar): Sir, I am extremely 
grateful to you for giving me the opportunity to make my Special Mention. 
Sir, I am raising a matter of great importance, namely, the complete crippl ing 
effect on the functioning of the local bodies and gram panchayats in the 
country, on account of non -holding of elections. Sir, as you are aware, article 
40 of the Constitution says "The State shall take steps to organise village 
panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be 
necessary to enable them to function as units of self -government." Sir, the 
73rd Amendment was made which led to far -reaching changes in article 243 
which clearly said " Every Panchayat, unless sooner dissolved u nder any law 
for the time being in force, shall continue for five years from the date 
appointed for its first meeting and no longer." The question of the Tenth 
Finance Commission has already been raised by my hon. friend, Mr. Reddy, I 
do not want to repeat that. But, Sir, that is a very serious question. As a result 
of these amendments to the Constitution, in many States, like Madhya 
Pradesh and others, local bodies are functioning .   But in other States, no 
election, either in respect of gram 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
panchayat or local bodies, has been held. I would particularly refer to my own 
State of Bihar where, since 1978, no election, either of gram panchayats or of 
municipality has been held. Sir, it is a very serious matter since there is  a 
judicial order of the High Court to hold the elections to gram panchayats and 
local bodies. The people are being denied of their right to self -governance. 
Besides, Sir, the people of the State of Bihar are also being denied of. the 
funds because, as per  the Tenth Finance Commission's recommendations, the 
money is to be released only to the panchayats and local bodies which are 
functional. We gather that as much as Rs. 400 crores is being lost every year 
by these municipal bodies and gram panchayats on account of the non-holding 
of elections. It is a very serious matter. It is a matter which ought to be taken 
notice of. I would request through you, Sir, the Government to kindly ensure 
that the complete case of violation of the constitutional mandate ought not to 
be resorted to and the people of Bihar must be given the opportunity, at the 
earliest, of self-Government. Thank you, Sir.

Period of Time). This was not acceptable to the U.S.A and, when there is a 
dispute between the parties like this, a reaso nable period of time is to be 
determined either by a bilateral agreement between the contesting parties or 
through an arbitrator. The arbitrator, normally, does not provide for more than 
15 months. After bilateral discussions to determine the time period, India and 
the U.S. signed a bi -lateral agreement on 28th December, 1999 Under this 
agreement, the final reasonable period of time will expire on 1st April, 2000. 
Out of the 1429 tariff lines, at the eight digit -level, on which Quantitative 
Restrictions were maintained by India on the grounds of balance of payments, 
under direct signing of the agreement, 714 items were removed on 1st April, 
2000 and the balance 715 by 1st April, 2001. As India has removed 
Quantitative Restrictions on 714, coinciding with the  Annual Exim Policy for

industry.

The next point which I would like to specially emphasis is dry land 
agriculture. Small and marginal farmers have to inherit this land from their 
ancestral property. As a result of the honest implementation of the Land 
Ceiling Act, there are some States which have done some excellent work. 
And because of that, some small and marginal farmers have got some land. 
Now they are totally out of this national endeavour of food 
production. Why are they not given loans from the District Cooperative Banks 
in the initial stages? When the District Cooperative Banks don't give them 
loans, ultimately, they have to approach the moneylenders. And, in fact, the 
moneylenders are charging a high rate of interest. They have the muscle 
power and, if by any chance, he were to fail in r epayment - which he is bound 
to, because of the floods, drought and other natural calamities -then, the 
moneylender makes the life of that man miserable. That is one of the reasons 
as to why so many farmers have gone to the extent of committing suicide - 
suicide is not any kind of pleasure - and nobody comes to his rescue. I was 
surprised when one of the Ministers happened to say that some psychiatrist 
should be sent to find out if there is some abnormality in his brain. This is a 
very cruel sort of joke that you are playing on them. These poor people are, in 
fact, very honest. They are prepared to pay each paisa of that money, but if it 
goes beyond their limit, and if moneylenders harass them to such an extent,

are really interested in doubling your production, then, you will have to 
encourage the involvement of these small and marginal farmers, and instead

seeds, good fertilizers and good

SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO (Andhra Pradesh) : Mr. Vice -
Chairman, Sir, thank you for giving me an opportunity. 
I rise to support the Budget on Agriculture Demands. 
India is predominantly an agriculture country, with 73% of its 
population consisting of farmers, agricult ure labourers, artisans, etc., who 
live on agriculture. Bapuji, rightly said, "India lives in its villages", and he 
was proud in saying that he is a kisan from Gujarat. But, Sir, even after 52 
years of independence, the provisions of basic services in rural areas, the 
heart of the nation, are far from satisfactory. Sir, 40% villages are without 
proper roads, 1.8 lakh villages do not have primary schools within one 
kilometre, and 4.5 lakh villages have drinking water problems. This is the 
rural scenario. And  even after 52 years of independence, we are not able to 
provide the basic minimum services. 
If we take India's agriculture, two -third is rain -fed and only one -
third is irrigated. So, there is every necessity to improve the rain -fed 
agriculture, as my other friends have also pointed out, to increase the 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [ 27 APRIL, 2000] 
production that would be sufficient to feed the teeming millions of the Indian 
population. If we talk about the production of foodgrains, it was 50 million 
tonnes when we b ecome independent, and now the production stands at 200 
million tonnes. This could be achieved because the farmers are innovative and 
they are ready to implement the new agro -economic practices given by the 
scientists. But what reward the farmer is getting  for this, except that he is 
being praised as Annadata. He has got his children to be educated, to be 
married, and he has also to take care of the health of the family. During the 
Green Revolution, a slogan was given, requesting farmers to "produce more 
or perish." Now, the farmers are not given full credit to their efforts. They are 
producing more and perishing also because of lack of remunerative prices. 
The farmers are responsible for the increase in food production and 
transforming the country from 'the  begging bowl to a bread basket.' 
Simultaneously, the country should realise the various constraints in 
production. Sir, various things have to be looked into, namery, supplying 
sufficient quantity of high -yielding variety of seeds, high cost of fertiliser s, 
scarcity of water, meeting the timely and sufficient credit needs of the 
farmers, etc. The credit requirement is to the tune of Rs. 44,635 crores, but 
only a credit of Rs. 41,800 crores is arranged. Sir, 90% of the farming 
community is indebted and their credit requirements are not met. They have to 
borrow at huge rates of interest from the private money -lenders. In 
agriculture, credit is an important input. If it is not met in time, the farmer will 
suffer. As Pandit Nehruji rightly said, "anything can wait, but not agriculture". 
Hence, the credit requirement of the farmers should be met amply. 
Regarding the Commission on Agricultural Costs and Prices, many 
of its members do not have any practical knowledge of agriculture. Those 
who have not seen the vill ages and do not know that a bund exists in the 
fields, are deciding the fate of the farming community. Sir, the real farmers 
should be there in the CACP. The CACP should announce the prices well in 
advance of the season, which has not been done so far. Cer tain realities which 
are involved in the process of agriculture should be taken into consideration 
while fixing the prices of agriculture commodities. 
There is every need for a crop insurance scheme throughout the 
country, for all the crops. The farmer dep ends on the vagaries of nature, and if 
there is no insurance protection for the crop he is raising, he will loose 
everything.   The farmer toils day-and- night, and his entire family is

mandals, while assessing the loss during times of damage. T he premium that 
has to be paid by the small and marginal farmers on account of this should

Agriculture Policy should be announced. The industrialists who form a small 
section of the population, are having an Industrial Policy since long back. But 
the farming community which constitutes the bulk of the population, has been 
deprived of this till today. The government should take immediate initiative 
to formulate a National Agri cultural Policy so that the farmers will have 
protection from all the vagaries of nature and that they will have a 
remunerative price etc. 
Our Chief Minister, Shri Chandra Babu Naidu, is giving a great 
thrust to agriculture in Andhra Pradesh by inducing the farmers to produce 
more by adopting new technologies and at a less cost. Many Kisan Melas are 
being held by the Agriculture Marketing Committees to bring awareness to 
the farming community. The Government has formed the Water -users 
Associations, and for the first time in the annals of the history of Andhra 
Pradesh, rights have been given to fanners to get water to their fields. Rs.142 
crores was allotted and spent. The channels were repaired in a very big way 
Because of this, water is reaching the tail -ends in time, as a  result of which, 
there is a bumper crop of paddy this year. 
When the price of chillies fell down last year, the Chief Minister 
took immediate steps for market intervention operations. Chillies from the 
fanners were purchased, and they wer e rescued to a great extent. Another 
important programme for the benefit of the farmers is the Water -shed 
Programme, and it has been taken up in a big way in Andhra Pradesh. Lakhs 
of acres of land is being brought under cultivation, and increased production 
has been made possible. Shri Anna Hazare, the social reformer from 
Maharashtra, visited Andhra Pradesh, saw the functioning of water -sheds and 
complemented our Chief Minister, Shri Chandra Babu Naidu, for making the 
running water work in a way that the precious top soil is not eroded.

Though the crop size is of 100 million tonnes, the production is to the tune of 
160 million kgs. The tobacco farmers are in d istress. At the instance of our 
Chief Minister and MPs, the Union Commerce Minister was pleased to make 
arrangements With the State Trading Corporation to buy tobacco at the last 
year's price plus 10 per cent. I am happy that the Central Government came to  
the rescue of the tobacco farmers. 
The cotton farmer is also in a miserable position. The crop has been 
lost in drought, and what little crop he has got is not fetching a good price. I 
request the Government to direct the Cotton Corporation of India to en ter the 
market, stay in the market and make purchases in a big way to help the farmer 
from being exploited by middlemen and traders. 
I am coming to a close, Sir. 
A word about fertilizers. The consumption of fertilizers in the year 
1961 was 0.21 million metric tonnes, whereas in 1999-2000, it was to the tune 
of 19.1 million metric tonnes. In countries like Japan, China etc. where the 
fertilizer consumption is more, the production is more. The recent hike in the

the Government to roll back the prices of fertilizers.  Otherwise, the 
production will go down.

Deserted Village, wherein he wrote: 
"Bold peasantry, the country's pride, When once
