economically viable. The other thing that we have to see is, if they are in 
difficulties, what kind of an assistance can be provided to them so that this 
very important section of the community is not put to a di sadvantaged position. 
Sir, this is a country -wide problem. Traditionally — and historically also - this 
handloom industry is a very important industry in this country. I do not want to 
go into the question of pride that we have always taken in the delicaci es and 
other wonderful things that this handloom industry has produced in this country 
all these years. This has been a very famous industry. I would like to mention 
that apart from Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and 
Madhya Pradesh, this industry is also flourishing in other States like Orissa 
and Rajasthan. It occupies a pivotal position in our economic life. 
Sir, despite the fact that from the First Five-Year Plan and till the 
Eighth Five-Year Plan, we are finding that there are always s ome suggestions, 
some measures, for promoting handloom, giving protection and trying to see 
as to how greater marketing can be done, yet it is unfortunate that nothing 
much has been done in this regard. Frankly, Sir, you will recall that a very 
senior and aged Member from Andhra Pradesh, Mr. Kotaiah, used to sit here.* 
Unfortunately, he is no more with us. He used to lament and bring to our notice 
with passion, with intensity and, I think, with the first -hand experience, what 
this industry has been going through, over the years. I think that should make 
us look at this industry in a broader perspective. 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [ 28 April, 2000 ] 
I also recall that the last committee, the Satyam Committee, was also 
referred to many a time in this House. At that time, the Report was not 
submitted. I have myself not seen the Report. The previous speaker, our friend 
from Andhra Pradesh, Mr. Radhakrishna Murty, has mentioned that, probabty, 
after Mr. Satyam, somebody else took over the chairmanship. I am not aware 
of that, and I have not seen the Report either. But I can say that this officer, 
Mr. Satyam, was the Textile Secretary. I even do not know where he is at the 
moment and what he is doing. But, having known him for some time, since he 
had worked with me, I can say  that he is certainly a person with both social 
concern and social conscience. 
Having said that, I say that I have not seen the Report. Probably, he 
might have been influenced by, what he himself said, "the imperatives or the 
compulsions of globalisation."  But that simple factor should not blind us, 
should not make us oblivious, to the social and economic realities in this 
country. On the other hand, we have also to think what measures and what 
safeguards we can devise to retrieve the situation and to see that this precious 
and valuable industry is really protected. So far as the employment potential is 
concerned, if I am right, this industry, with such an immence potential, 
probably, may be next only to agriculture. Then, we have to take all measures. 
It is  also unfortunate that the Handloom Board which was set up 
years back with very laudable objectives, has got ritualised. It got -I hate to use 
the word-bureaucratised, in the sense that somehow or other, more questions 
were asked than going into the results , and the performance was ignored. I 
think, it fell into some kind of a trap, and, that is why, it has really outlived its 
utility. Something much more drastic has to be done. Ministers are taking note 
of what the hon. Members are saying. I am not aware of  the reaction of the 
Textile Ministry and the Textile Minister after having read the Report. 
But, Sir, I have seen at least two Reports on this, the Sivaraman 
Committee Report and the Mira Seth Committee Report. I think, these Reports 
were also on the right lines. Probably, they laid down the guidelines for us, by 
which we could take care of the obligations of liberalisation or the compulsions 
of liberalisation and, at the same time, strengthen the handloom industry in the 
country. 
244 

[ 28 April, 2000 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, in the first place, I do not see much of a confrontation between 
the powerloom sector and the handloom sector. The only thing is that one is 
comparatively weaker than the other. The powerloom sector has been, 
unfortunately, taken over, not by the persons who were in the powerloom 
sector or who were directly concerned with it, but by more powerful interests. 
That is why, this powerful sector should not be allowed to do the arm -twisting 
or to put the handloom sector to a disadvantage. 
Both the industries have a place, from the point of view of foreign 
market. Sir, you will recall that this industry in the Madras Presidency had 
earned a name for itself throughout the world, particularly, in the Western 
world. That is why I say when we could make it at a time when we were at a 
disadvantaged position, from various angles, why and how is it that we have 
not been able to give the proper support to the handloom industry to grow? 
Though we do not like the word "protection", yet we have to protect and 
support the weaker and vulnerable sections and make this industry 
economically viable. Only when they are economically viable, the question of 
their vulnerability, from the point of view of social justice etc. will not be there. 
That is why I suggest that t he Government should come to the House with a 
clear policy statement, taking into account the place that this industry has 
occupied throughout the history of this country. I am afraid 1 do not find myself 
in agreement with the suggestions made by the last Committee that every kind 
of support to this industry must be withdrawn. If it is done it will be a disastrous 
step. For years we have been saying they should be given credit at cheaper 
rates, besides other concessions. I think we have to think on those li nes. Sir, I 
support the suggestions given by the Mira Seth Committee that there should 
be a National Credit Fund for them. I think this valuable suggestion has been 
taken into account in a different form by the mover of the Bill. 
Sir, withdrawal of facilit ies and concessions to this industry will cut at 
the roots of the handloom industry. This industry is, by and large, concerned 
with the poor people. It is really the workers' industry, wherein the family 
workers are not fully employed. On the one hand, we should see that no 
unnecessary burden is put on the industry, and on the other, the watchful 
Government should ensure that all kinds of concessions and facilities are 
provided to the needy sections. It should also ensure that these people 
because of their economic disparity are not exploited by the sharks who have 
now taken over the powerloom inudstry.    There also we have to 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [ 28 April, 2000 ] 
balance the two particular factors. So far as research and development is 
concerned, this is an extremely important area and this was supposed to be 
one of the responsibilities for the handloom industry. I would like to state that 
most of the State Governments and Departments dealing with handloom 
industry have failed in the area of research and development. Research and 
Development is extremely important, from the point of view of quality, and 
quality has something to do with marketing. Apart from that, we have to explore 
new markets for this industry. 
Then, suggest to these poor people, who are depr ived of those 
facilities, what kind of a cloth they should make, what kind of a design they 
should adopt and so on. I think this task has been neglected, though, I am not 
fully aware of the recent position in the States. But, earlier, there were a 
number of institutions of this kind. It seems they also lost their moorings. 
Probably, their working got ritualised. 
That is why I think that another very important area which needs to be 
focussed is research and development, in order to improve their quality, 
improve their marketing prospects. Only then, they can face competition; and 
produce handloom cloth according to the taste of the people. Mr. Vice-
Chairman, without taking much of your time, I would like to submit that there is 
a change all over the world. There is a change in the taste of the people. They 
don't want synthetic clothes. On the other hand, handloom articles are a rage in 
the Western countries. When we go abroad, we give small presents to the 
people. They are accepted. They are highly welcomed. I  think, these factors 
also should be taken into account. The easy path that we sometimes adopt is 
not something which really behoves this country with such hory traditions of 
handloom industry. 
Sir, I fully agree with the proposal for handloom mart . This is also one 
of the ways and methods of publicising the handloom ; and many efforts have 
been made in this direction, very successfully, though, in a limited way, for 
small-scale industries at different places. So far as the handloom industry is 
concerned, this is a kind of facility which the Government has not provided. If 
they provide this facility to this sector, then, we can say that they have really 
discharged their duty to this sector. Mr. Reddy, the Mover of the Bill, has 
suggested a Handloom Weavers'  Welfare Fund , on the lines of the 
Development Fund, National Credit Fund,  suggested by the Mira  Seth 
Committee.   Yes, I am for a Handloom 
246 

[ 28 April, 2000 ] RAJYA SABHA 
Weavers' Welfare Fund. But our economic policy, our industrial policy, should 
be so devised, should be so fine-tuned that this handloom industry is made to 
stand in competition with any other sector. When I say 'with any other sector', I 
only mean that when unfair methods are adopted by other sectors and 
elsewhere, the vulnerabilit y, the difficulties, of this section have also to be 
taken into account so that they really do not need the help of this welfare fund; 
there is not much of a need to draw upon this welfare fund. However, a 
welfare fund is necessary for every section, whether it is the Government 
servants or any other section, for meeting particular contingencies and 
emergencies. This should be done. When the Ministry is considering a 
committee, it is high time they take into account the experience of the 
handloom industry, what has been said by various committees, from time to 
time. They should take note of the suggestions that were made, and how far 
they were implemented, in accordance with various Plan documents. 
With regard to the handloom industry, they should come out w ith a 
policy statement. which should really help, strengthen and perpetuate the 
stability of the handloom industry. With these words, Mr. Vice-Chairman, I 
thank you. I do hope that this can be possible if the Textile Minister convenes 
a meeting of the vari ous State Textile Ministers because this is also an area 
where divided responsibility, unfortunately, only spells doom.If there is a 
proper realisation of the joint responsibilities of both the Union Government 
and the State Governments, I think a realty f unctional and forward-looking 
approach to make the handloom industry viable can be adopted. 
With these words, Sir, I support Mr. Reddy's Bill.  Thank you.

RAJYA SABHA [ 28 April, 2000 ] 
5.00 P.M. 
STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Match- Fixing in Cricket 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION AND MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI 
SUKH DEV SINGH DHJNDSA): The iss ue of match-fixing has been at the 
centre-stage of media reporting for the last few weeks. It has also been 
debated in the two Houses of Parliament. I have already made statements in 
both the Houses of Parliament on this issue. In my statement, I had menti oned 
that Government will not hesitate to initiate an inquiry in the matter of match-
fixing by any agency of the Government, as required. On the basis of several 
news-items in prominent magazines and newspapers of the country, as also 
the statement of prominent cricket administrators and players, there is need to 
inquire into the matter further. Government believes that those who are guilty 
must be punished, those who are innocent must not be slandered, those who 
have evidence must cooperate and shall be gi ven adequate protection, and 
those who make ill founded allegations must be exposed. Keeping in view the 
sentiments expressed by hon. Members in both Houses of Parliament, the 
sensitivity of the case and the complexities involved, as also the issue of 
jurisdiction, Government has decided to entrust the matter to CBI for 
appropriate inquiry and necessary action. During the discussions in Parliament 
on this issue, the pre-dominant view was also to entrust this inquiry to the CBI. 
It is hoped that this inquiry  will clear the air of rumours and suspicion 
surrounding this subject. The case already registered by the Delhi Police under 
FIR No. 111/2000 against Hansie Cronje and others will be pursued by Delhi 
Police to its logical conclusion.

investigation, I think no clarifications should be sought otherwise it will affect.

under the Brahmaputra Board Act, 1980 for planning and implementation of 
measures for the management of floods and bank erosion in Brahmaputra valley.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNI -
CATIONS (SHRI TAPANI SIKDAR) (a) Postal services in the entire country 
including rural areas arc provided by the Department of Posts as per provisions 
of Indian Post Office Act. 1898 and Rules framed thereunder According to 
these statutory provisions, the Department of Posts has monopoly in the matter 
of letter mail articles only. 
(b) and (c) Extra Departmental Agents (EDAs) numbering 3,09. 915 as 
on 31- 3-99 arc responsible for the entire rural postal not work Comprising 
1.28.193 ED Post Offices in the country, The Extra-Departmental System which 
is more than a century old has proved its worth as a practical and viable method 
of extending basic postal facilities to rural areas where due to inadequate work-
load full-fledged departmental posts offices cannot be set up. The ED Agents 
arc engaged on specific terms and conditions which vary significantly from' 
those of regular Govt employees. ED Agents arc required to work for a period 
of 2 to 5 hours per day only and it is necessary for them to have alternate source 
of independent livelihood. Being local residents of the post village or the 
delivery jurisdiction of the Branch Post Office, they enjoy accep tability in the 
local community they serve. ED Post Office provides all basic postal services 
including agency functions which arc of benefit to the rural population and 
help in socio-economic development 
Terms and conditions of engagement for ED Agents ha ve been revised 
from time to time by the Government progressively extending allowances and 
other payments on pro-rata and resulting in additional benefits for ED Agents 
In the context of setting up of the Vth Central pay Commission Tor regular 
Central Gove rnment employees, the Government had set up a one man 
committee headed by Justice Charanjit Talwar, retired judge. Delhi High Court 
to examine the wage structure and service condition of ED Agents and the 
Committee submitted its report to the Government on  30-4-97. After due 
consideration of the recommendations of justice Talwar Committee, the 
Government extended a package of benefits to ED Agents in full and final 
settlement of all pending demands relating to implementation of just ice Talwar 
Committee's recommendations. This package of benefits extended through the 
order of Department of Posts dated 17-12-98 provided the following additional 
benefits lor the ED Agents:—  
(i) Payment of arrears for the period 1 -1-1996 to 28- 2-1998 by 
increasing the basic allowance of ED Agents by multiplying it with 
a factor of 3.25 
57 

RAJYA SABHA (02 MAY, 20001 
(ii) Introduction of Time -Related Continuity Allowance (TRCA) on the 
pattern of first two scales of pay recommended by the Justice Talwar 
Committee for each category of ED Agents (except ED SPMs for 
which only one TRCA). 
(iii) Provision of paid leave for 10 days for each half year, without the 
facility of earn- forward. 
(iv) Increased limit of ex -gratia gratuity for ED Agents from Rs. 6000/ - 
to Rs 18.000/-. 
(v) Increased amount of Office maintenance Allowance from Rs. 25/-per 
month to Rs. 50/- per month for EDBPMs. and EDSPMs. 
(vi) Payment of lumpsum Severance Amount of Rs. 20.000/ - or Rs. 
30.000/- depending on period of employ ment of ED Agents, on 
demitting office at the age of 65 years or after absorption against 
regular departmental post, as a form of post employment benefits. 
Recommendations made by justice Talwar Committee also including those for 
rationalising the ED system, reducing the number of ED Agents and also capping 
future growth of the system. But appreciating the relevance of the ED System for 
the rural postal network and its social benefits. Government have not implemented 
these recommendations. The Government's policy therefore, ensures full justice to 
the interest of ED Agents. The benefits extended to the ED As through order dated 
17-12-98 were then estimated to involve recurring additional annual expenditure of 
Rs. 301.35 crores, over and above an amount of Rs. 157.74 crores on account of 
payment of arrears for the period of 1 -1 -96 to 28-2-98. 
Improving the terms and conditions of engagement of Extra Departmental 
Agents including the prospects of eligible ED Agents for absorption against 
regular vacancies is a continuing exercise. Existing rules of recruitment for the cadres 
of Postman. Postal Assistant/Sorting Assistant and Grade "D" already provide for 
preference to eligible ED Agents for recruitment against departmental post.

3857. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD : Will the Minister of

money orders. The norms varies from within 48 hours to 120 hours, exclud ing

areas, it may take a little longer. These broad norms arc subject to mail

bution arc given below :—  
— Close monitoring of the collection, transm ission, processing and 
delivery of mails both at the field and Directorate levels;

mail transmission at transit mail offices in the Metro and oth er 
important cities. 
— Mechanisation of delivery through the use of mopeds.

Time Limit for Sanction of Schemes for Units Registered with BIFR 
3871. MISS FRIDA TOPNO: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have any plan to prescribe time limit for sanction 
of scheme after a unit is registered under BIFR; 
(b) whether RBI has any plan to relax provisions of non-performing assets 
in case of industries registered with BIFR which require immediate and urgent 
infusion of f unds for operations of the units to avoid any lay off, closure of 
suspension of production; and 
(c) whether in such cases BIFR would issue instructions to Banks to allow 
operation of Bank accounts in order to maintain production for arresting cash 
losses ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL) : (a) The cases registered with Board for 
Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) are dealt with in accordance 
with the provisions of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 
1985. Section 18(1) of the Act lays down that the Operating Agency shall prepare 
Rehabilitation proposal as expeditiously as possible and ordinarily within a 
period of 90 days. 
(b) Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has reported that at present, there is no 
proposal to relax provisioning norms in respect of Non- Performing Assets 
(NPAs) of Industries registered with BIFR. 
(c) As per the scheme of SICA, BIFR has no jurisdiction to issue 
instructions to the banks to allow holding on operations in their accoun ts. 
However, in certain cases, on the requests received from the companies, the 
Board has advised the concerned banks to allow such holding on operations so 
that the financial position of the sick industries does not deteriorate further. 
Rural Credit 
3872 SHRI H. K. JAVARE GOWDA : Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that even after the enhancement of corpus fund in 
rural credit, the poor cultivators are not benefited ; and 
90 

[02 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefore? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL) : (a) and (b) No, Sir. It is not correct 
to say that the cultivators/agriculturists are not benefited. Ever since the 
introduction of Special Agric ultural Credit Plans (SACPs) for public sector 
banks by the Reserve Bank of India since 1994 -95, the ground level flow of 
credit to agriculture has increased from Rs. 8255 crore in 1994 -95 to Rs. 
17787.63 crore in the year 1998- 99. The public sector banks have projected 
an agregate target of Rs. 21307.62 crore for disbursement to agriculture under 
SACP during the year 1999- 2000. The achievements for the year are under 
review. Meanwhile, RBI and National Bank for Agriculture and Rural 
Development have been t aking several measures to further strengthen the 
flow of credit to agriculture sector. Some of these steps include introduction 
of cash credit facility for meeting the composite credit requirements of 
farmers/cultivators, introduction of the Kisan Credit C ard Scheme for 
agricultural borrowers, opening of specialized agricultural branches to take 
care of financing of high -tech agricultural products, simplification of loan 
application forms, delegation of powers to the branch managers of banks for 
speedier sanction of loan, insistence of no -due certificate by banks at their 
own discretion, non- insistence of security/ margin for agricultural loans upto 
Rs. 10,000/- etc. In addition, banks falling short of their target in lending to 
agriculture have to contribut e to Rural Infrastructure Development Fund 
(RIDF) maintained by National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development 
(NABARD) for assisting the State Governments and State -owned 
Corporation for completion of their on- going projects relating to rural 
infrastructure.

STATEMENT 
I. Cental Water Comnussion 
 
The Central Water Commission is charged with the general responsibility  of 
initiating, coordinating and furthering in consultation with the  
StateGovernments concerned, schemes for the control, conservation and 
utilisation of water resources throughout the country for the purpose of flood 
manager irrigation, navigation, drinking water supply and water power 
generation. The Commission will, if so requires also undertake the  construction 
and execution   of any such scheme In exercise of these responsibilities the 
Central Water Commission is performing the following function:- 
                 1. To make all necessary investigations and surveys and when so  
                      required, to prepare schemes and designs for the development of 
 
149 

RAJYA SABHA [ 02 MAY, 2000] 
river valleys in respect of power generation, irrigation by gravity flow or 
lift, navigation, flood management, environmenta l management, 
rehabilitation and resettlement, soil conservation, anti-water logging 
measures, reclamation of alkaline and saline soils, drainage and other 
related facilities such as malaria control, recreation and fish culture 
and —  for drinking water supply; 
2. to undertaken construction work of any river valley development scheme 
on behalf of the Government of India or State Governments concerned; 
3. to advise and assist, when so required, the State Governments 
(Commissions, Corporations or Boards that may be set up) in the 
investigation, surveys and preparation of river valley and power 
developoment schemes for particular areas and regions; 
4. to advise the Government of India in respect of Water Resources 
Development, rights and disputes as between different States which affect 
any scheme for the conservation and utilization of water may have on the 
interests of the concerned States and any matter that may be referred to 
the Commission in connection with river valley development; 
5. to advise the Central Government and State Governments on the basin-
wise development of water resources; 
6. to advise the Government of India in regard to all matters relating to 
Inter-State water disputes; 
7. to advise the Government of India in regard to the settlement of 
priorities for plant, materials and foreign exchange as between various 
river valley development schemes and monitoring of projects; 
8. to collect, coordinate the collection of, publish and analyse the data relating 
to water ways, tidal rivers, rainfall, runoff and temperature, ground water 
resources, silting of reservoirs, behaviour of hydraulic structures, 
environmental aspects etc. 
9. to collect, maintain and publish statistical data relating to water 
resources and its utilization including quality of water throughout India 
and to act as the Central Bureau of Information relating to water 
resources; 
150 

[02 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
. 10. to initiate schemes and arrange for the training of Indian Engineers in 
India and abroad in all aspects of river valley development and also 
coordinate the training activities in the State Government Institutions; 
11. to standardize instruments, methods of observation and record, 
materials and construction, design and operation of irrigation projects; 
12. to initiate studies on socio -agro-economic and ecolo gical aspects of 
irrigation projects for the sustained development of irrigation; 
13. to conduct and coordinate research on the various aspects of river 
valley development schemes such as flood management, irrigation, 
navigation, water power development etc. and the connected structural 
and design features; 
14. to promote modern data collection techniques, such as remote sensing 
satellite technology for water resources development and flood 
forcasting and development of computer software's; 
15. to conduct studies on da m safety aspects for the existing and future 
dams and standardize the instruments for the dam safety measures; 
16. to initiate the morphological studies, river behaviour, bank erosion/ 
coastal erosion problems and advise the Central and State Governments 
on all such matters, 
17. to conduct experiments, research and generally to carry out such other 
activities as will promote economic and optimum utilization of water 
resources; and 
18. to promote and create mass awareness in the progress and achievements 
made by the country in water resources development. 
II. Water and power consultancy services (I) limited 
1. Water and Power Consultancy Services (India) Limited (WAPCOS) 
is a Government of India Undertaking established in 1969 to provide 
consultancy services in the spher e of Planning and Development 
of Water Resources, Sector comprising of Irrigation, Agriculture, 
Flood Control, Ground Water exploitation, Environment, Socio-
economic studies and power Sector comprising of Hydro, power 
large and Mini Thermal and Transmissio n/Distribution systems. 
WAPCOS undertakes assignments from feasibility to design of

operation and maintenance The Company has diversified its 
activities' into areas like environmental engineering, water supply, 
sewerage, ports and harbour and dam safety surveillance, system 
engineering and info mation technologies, sanitation etc Recently, 
the company has decided to undertake turn key assignments 
including construction of projects for small Hydro Power 
Development water harvesting etc. 
2. The consultancy services are rendered through its  own personnel 
and expertise available from its constituents and various special i zed

3958. MISS MABEL REBELLO : Will the Minister of WATER  
RESOURCES be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that the country suffer enormous human and 
material losses due to excess water floods and also from drought  and  lack of 
rain and that precious water goes to sea and we loose it forever; 
(b) whether Government are seriously considering about conserving 
precious rain water as Scientists have forecasted that India in the  next  
Millennuini will face the worst drought ever in the world; and  
(c) whether Government have taken any viable measures to avoid this  
calamity which may fell the country in the near future and millions of people

156 

[02 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY O F WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY) : (a) to (c) Rainfall 
in the country is highly variable both in time and space. This results in floods in 
some parts of the country, whereas the other parts arc affected by droughts. 
About 40  +7Mha of the area in the country is flood prone whereas 51.13 Mha 
is drought prone. On an average 7.5 Mha area is affected annually by floods 
with average damages of the order of Rs. 1,155 crore. On an average 1, 529 
human lives are lost due to floods. India receives an average annual rainfall of 
about 4000 Billion Cubic Meter (BCM) including snow. Out of this, 3, 000 
BCM occurs during monsoon resulting in an average annual flow of about 1869 
BCM in the various rivers of the country. The utilisable runoff by 
conventional methods has been assessed as 690 Billion Cubic Meter (BCM). 
A live storage capacity of 176.73 BCM has been created by construction of 
large dams upto 1995 including about 3 BCM capacity created by medium & 
small dams. Projects to add an additional capacity of about 75.42 BCM are under 
construction and 132.32 BCN are under planning. Out of 432 BCM of 
replenishable ground water, 260 BCM has been tapped. In order to complete 
the ongoing projects, Government is providing Central Loan Assistance 
underAccelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme. The National Water Policy 
(1987) stipulates that drinking water requirement should be the first charge on 
any available water. In addition, Command Area Development Programme is 
being implemented to fully utilize the potential created. 
Government of India is also promoting Rain Water Harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, Artificial Recharge of Ground Water and 
roof-top rain water harvesting under the Sector reform Project of Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural Development for 
which technical and financial assistance is provided to the State Government 
and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water Board has also taken 
up pilot studies for artificial ground water recharge.

3961 SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news -item 
captioned 'Water pricing authority proposed" as published in the Times of 
India dated 2nd December, 1999; 
(b) if so. whether the National Commission on Water Resources has 
recommended reforms and changes in the laws relating to water policy, 
(c) if so, the details of recommendations made by the Commission, and 
(d) to what extent Government have accepted the recommendations and 
changes in the proposed water pricing authority have been made ? 
THE MINISTER OF  STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY) : (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The National Commission for Integrated Water Resources 
Development has recommended for enactment of a law on Inter-State rivers to 
be called the Inter-State Rivers and River Valley (Integrated and Participatory 
Management) Act to interalia provide for (i) the constitution of River Basin 
Organisation and for their powers and functions and (ii) data collection and 
studies to be made by Union for possible Inter-State inter-basin transfer. It has 
also recommended to amend the Inter State Water Disputes Act, 1956 to ensure 
that awards of Inter-State water tribunals are given within a resonable period of 
time as also for the effectiveness of such awards. It has emphasised the need for 
revising the National Water Policy, 1987. 
159 

RAJYA SABHA [ 02 MAY, 2000] 
(c) Statement is attached (See below) 
(d) An implementation Cell in the National Water Development Agency 
has been constituted to examine recommendations of the National Commission, 
including the recommendation regarding water pricing authority, and suggest 
to union Government about the implementability or other -wise of the 
recommendations and to suggest modalities for implementation of such 
recommendations, as found implementable. An Advisory Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Chairman, Central Water Commission has been constituted 
for assisting the implementation Cell in examining the recommendations. 
STATEMENT 
The main recommendations of the National Commission for Integrated 
Water Resources Development are as under :—  
1. Continued Government funding on enhanced scale for major 
projects, instilling financial discipline and prioritisation of projects 
for channelising the funds. Central assistance to major projects to 
be project-wise instead of being part of the overall plan assistance. 
2. Need for well laid down compensation packages for all categories of 
project affected persons. While doing so, the Commission has 
emphasised that resettlement and rehabilitation projects be 
implemented by a functional authority with sufficient funds. 
3. Need for amending the existing Inter -State Water Disputes Act, 
1956, enactment of a new Act in lieu of the existing River Board's 
Act, 1956, and also amending the existing Irrigation Acts which 
would facilitate participatory irrigation management. 
4. Optimal utilisation of land and water should be aimed at in basins 
having surplus before considering interbasin transfers (intrabasin 
transfer to be given first priority). 
5. Setting up of River Basin Organisation for  each Inter -State River 
having representation from the concerned State Governments, 
Water Users etc. 
6. Substantial revision of present water rates to cover the entire 
operation & maintainance expenses, constituting Water Pricing 
Authority on the analogy of existing Energy Pricing Authorities. 
160 

[02 MAY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
7. For Environment protection, the principle of "User Pays, Polluter Pays" 
need to be adopted for industrial uses. 
8. Need for reviewing the National Water Policy (1987), need for making 
hydrological data for all basins freely available to all interested. 
9. For flood control measures, Commission has recommended 
preparation of disaster preparedness plans, performance review of 
embankments and policy to regulate the land use in different flood zones. 
Existing flood forcecasting system be strengthened and modernised 
using telemetry and satellite communication. 
 
10. For optimal and integrated development of trans— Himalayan rivers, India 
should work for cooperation amongst the neighbouring countries. For 
this purpose, it has been suggested that National Water Development Agency 
(NWDA) in India, Water Resource Planning Organisations (WARPO) in 
Bangladesh and Energy Development Authority (EDA) in Nepal be 
designated to interact as a clearing house of information. 
11. For hydropower development, Commission has recommended creation 
of hydropower development fund, promotion of joint ventures, tariff 
rationalisation etc. 
12. For navigation development, the Commission has recommended that Inland 
Water Transport be treated as a nascent industry.

DR. RAJA RAMANNA (Nominated): Sir, it is with great sadness that 
I take part in this debate on Air India. In the earlier days, we used to be so 
proud of our national carrier and it was thought to be a part of our 
Independence Movement. In those days, our airline system was among the 
best in the world. We used to be so proud of it. At that time, the Chairman was 
no less a person than Mr. J.R.D. Tata. Now, as the years go by, it is easy to 
forget Mr. Tata. But we have seen him in action, in running the various 
industries of the country and in looking after Air India. He was not a full time 
Chairman. We were very proud of the fact that Air India was by far the best 
airline in the world. We did ask  him once: How do you manage to keep Air 
India at such a high position? And we were very surprised with the reply that 
he gave. He said, "I give top priority to maintenance." People think that it is 
the management, or. sending off the files quickly. or. the amount of money 
involved, that is important. But you must appoint the right people to see that 
the plane is maintained regularly and the signals are checked regularly. When 
a plane comes down, it should come down with a natural safety. The people 
had a kind of pride in running these planes. This was obvious to all of us who 
travelled in those days. Everybody was polite on the plane. Even the 
passengers wanted to look after the plane and not mess it up. as they do it 
now. All this comes about due to a widespread lack of morale. If something 
goes wrong, everything starts going wrong and even the passengers become 
a nuisance, as it happened in recent times. But I would like to bring to the 
attention of the people that simply saying that the management is bad,  will not 
do. Management can be wonderful, but the management has to be built up. I 
can give you hundreds of instances where planes have flown empty and 
ticketing people have been rude to me and say that we cannot take you even 
when I have a reservation . But the basic malaise must be understood. For 
instance. Mr. Tata was ignominiously removed from the Chairmanship by no 
less than a great Prime Minister like Mr. Morarji Desai. There was a strange 
reason for  it.     He said.  "We should have a chairman  who is

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Explosion of Ammunitions in the Ammunition Depot, Bharatpur 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): Sir, 
Ammunition Depot, Bharatpur was established during the period 1957- 65 and 
is located approximately six kms. from Bharatpur town. This Depot holds parts 
of Southern Command Reserve and some portions of Army Headquarters 
Reserve ammunition. The Depot was holding approximately 30,000 tonnes of 
ammunition under both permanent (17,220 metric tonnes) as well as non 
standard storage (12,700 metric tonnes). 
The sequence of events as reported by the Army Headquarters is as 
follows:- 
229 

[ 02 May, 2000 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) The fire had started at approximately 1530 hrs. on 28th 
April, 2000, from outside the perimeter wall. 
(b) High temperatures ranging from 45 to 47 degrees Celsius 
and prevailing strong South Westerly winds aided the rapid 
spread of fire to the open plinths. 
(c) The explosion and fire continued unabated throu ghout the 
night of 28/29 April, 2000. The periodicity of explosion 
gradually reduced during the day on 29th April, 2000. 
Finally, the fire was brought under control by the evening of 
29th April, 2000. There has been no explosion since 2200 
hours on 29th April, 2000. 
(d) The Chief of Staff, Headquarters Corps located at Mathura 
was asked to coordinate fire fighting efforts and all available 
resources at Bharatpur, and additional resources from 
Alwar, Agra and Mathura were placed at his disposal. 
While detailed assessment is being made separately, on 29th April, 
2000, the area was reconnoitered. It is confirmed that ammunition stores in 20 
Open Plinths and 9 affected sheds weighing approximately 12111 MT and 
costing about Rs.376 crores was lost. In addition, infrastructure of replacement 
cost of approximately Rs. 13 crores has also been destroyed/damaged. The 
ammunition in the remaining storage sheds is prima facie safe but this would 
need confirmation after detailed inspection. 
Types of Ammunition Stored in this depot are (a) Air Defence 
Missiles (b) Anti Tank Guided Missiles (c) Artillery ammunition of all types (d) 
Tank and BMP ammunition (e) Small Arms ammunition, and (f) Mines and 
explosives. 
As per information available, 2 civilians died and 7 were injured. The 
State Government have been asked by the Ministry for a report on damage to 
life and property. They are in the process of surveying this damage and have 
informed the Ministry on 1.5.2000 that their report will be sent in about a 
week's time. Compensation will be paid for the damages caused, within 7 
days of receipt of proposal from the Government of Rajasthan.  Three Army 
personnel have also been suffered minor injuries.

The following steps have been taken: - (i) Court of I nquiry under a 
Major General has been constituted; (ii) Adequate qualified personnel to 
inspect remaining ammunition sheds in the depot have been ordered to be 
moved. 
The existing security and safety guidelines are: - (a) A broad policy 
letter regarding pre cautions to be taken to prevent fire accidents with the 
onset of summer was issued on 28th April, 1997, and repromulgated on 17th 
April, 2000. (b) Each ammunition depot has its own security and fire fighting 
instructions which are updated periodically, (c)  Annual inspections are 
undertaken by technical as well as administrative heads, (d) Between 1996-97 
up to 31.3.2000, Rs. 241. 73 crores were allocated for building standard 
storage accommodation. Out of this, Rs. 126.25 crores were sanctioned in 
1999-2000.
